Panthers vs Packers prediction, pick against the spread and over/under for Thursday Night Football: Green Bay was flirting with record warmth this week, and the Lambeau forecast is clear, mid-fifties and close to calm at kickoff, so neither offense gets to blame the frozen tundra. The spread says Green Bay by 3.5. I say that is a field goal and a hook of respect for a home team that has scored 144 points and allowed 145.

Carolina Panthers (3-3) at Green Bay Packers (4-3), 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Prime Video, the last kickoff of the year on daylight time before the clocks fall back Sunday. The consensus has Green Bay −3.5 with a total of 47.5 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: Carolina Panthers +3.5, Under 47.5, and a final of Packers 24, Panthers 22.

The Carolina side exists because Green Bay hasn't separated from anybody. Seven games, 144 scored, 145 allowed, a point differential of minus one. Carolina has scored 159 and allowed 166 in six games and is 2-1 on the road. This is a coin flip wearing a field goal and a hook.

The Formula: Net ratings Green Bay Packers −3.5, Carolina Panthers −1.5 (nflverse play-by-play, Oct 28, 2026).

The injury report is where this game changed. Green Bay ruled out guard Travis Glover and center Sean Rhyan, so two of the men in the middle of Jordan Love's protection won't be there Thursday night. The Packers are also without linebacker Zaire Franklin, and receiver Matthew Golden is questionable. Losing two interior blockers on a short week is not how a team lays more than a field goal comfortably.

Carolina got hit too. The Panthers ruled out guards Damien Lewis and Torricelli Simpkins III, linebacker Jaelan Phillips and cornerback Akayleb Evans. Bryce Young was a full participant, but he faces a loud building on a short week behind a patched-up front of his own.

The Under holds even without wind, because this Green Bay offense lives at about three touchdowns a game, 144 points in seven. The Formula's number is about 49, and my final is 46, a point and a half shy of the posted 47.5. Two patched-up offensive fronts and two teams on four days of rest is not a recipe for fireworks.

The room mostly agrees with me on the side. The Formula has Panthers 25, Packers 24, an outright Carolina win, and Next Man Up has Packers 23, Panthers 22, well inside the number. Letdown Watch is the lone dissenter at Packers 25, Panthers 20, and it would happily lay the points with Green Bay. In The Trenches has no pick. Follow The Money has no pick.

Carolina doesn't need to win at Lambeau. It needs to keep a Green Bay offense missing two interior blockers inside a field goal and a hook. That's the game I see, a one-score night decided late, with the Packers winning it and the Panthers getting the money.

Packers 24, Panthers 22. Panthers cover the 3.5. Under 47.5.

games.fanatic_story:
Carolina Panthers vs Green Bay Packers opens Week 8 on Thursday night at Lambeau Field after Green Bay spent Wednesday chasing a record high, with a clear, mid-fifties kickoff forecast that counts as a heat wave up here in late October. Packers fan Paul Lindgren calls the weather a courtesy to guests, and Panthers fan Mitch Kovac, who flew in braced for the frozen tundra, calls it a trap. Carolina comes in at 3-3, Green Bay at 4-3, both teams on a short week, 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Prime Video, the last kickoff before the clocks fall back. Paul is in shirtsleeves, guarding the Packers' ledger of championships like the wind might take it. Mitch showed up in a parka out of pure suspicion.

Mitch: Paul, I packed for the frozen tundra. You people sold me a brochure.

Paul: The tundra takes Thursdays off when company comes. Go stand by the Titletown stage before the game. Ha Ha Clinton-Dix and Jarrett Bush are the alumni up there tonight. Two guys who made a living taking the football away from quarterbacks.

Mitch: I'll shake their hands and show them my depth chart. They'll want to see how a roster gets built.

Paul: Built? Mitch, we have a ledger. Thirteen league championships. Eleven came before the merger, and four Super Bowls, the first two, then XXXI and XLV, and nobody in this county counts the overlap twice.

Mitch: You recite it like a grocery list you learned at your grandmother's knee.

Paul: I did learn it at her knee. She also taught me Herb Adderley, Jerry Kramer, Willie Davis and LeRoy Butler, in that order, before I could ride a bike.

Mitch: And I learned Julius Peppers. Drafted in Charlotte, raised in Charlotte, carried into the Hall of Fame. Carolina won the NFC South last season the same way, from the inside out. Dan Morgan built this roster front first, and Derrick Brown is the proof.

Paul: Lovely speech. Look at our season, though. Seven games, 144 points scored, 145 allowed. We're 2-1 at home. We have been walking a tightrope since September.

Mitch: A tightrope with a one-point hole in it. My guys have scored 159 and allowed 166 in six, and we're 2-1 on the road. We travel, Paul. We like your stadium.

The real argument tonight is up front, and the official injury report gave both of them ammunition. Green Bay will be without guard Travis Glover and center Sean Rhyan, the two men in the middle of Jordan Love's protection, plus linebacker Zaire Franklin. Receiver Matthew Golden is questionable. Carolina ruled out guards Damien Lewis and Torricelli Simpkins III, linebacker Jaelan Phillips and cornerback Akayleb Evans. Bryce Young was a full participant all week, and Love isn't on the report at all.

Mitch: Two of the people who snap and block for Love are out. Matt LaFleur and Adam Stenavich will be drawing protections on a napkin by halftime.

Paul: Napkins are for brats, Mitch. And two of your guards are out too. So are your linebacker and your corner. We can count that high in Brown County.

Mitch: Then count my sacrifices. Back home in NoDa, the neighbors are decorating houses for the NoDaWeen contest. Hodges Family Farm closes its pumpkin patch for the year on Saturday. I'm missing all of it to sit on your porch.

Paul: You're missing it for history. Both defenses play a 3-4 base front, Ejiro Evero's for you and Jonathan Gannon's for us. Love started at Detroit, Young started at home against Tampa Bay.

Mitch: Fine. Ask me the question you always ask.

Paul: Super Bowl trophies since your first season?

Mitch: None yet. Two NFC titles, a division banner from last year and a locker room of players we drafted ourselves. Ask again in February.

Paul: I'll write your answer in pencil. The ledger only takes ink for titles.

Mitch: Keep the pencil sharp. And lend me a sweatshirt for the fourth quarter. Even a heat wave in Green Bay goes cold after dark.

Paul hands Mitch a sweatshirt with a G on it. Mitch puts it on inside out, and they walk toward the gate in weather nobody in Brown County will admit was pleasant.

My call: Packers 24, Panthers 22.

Ravens vs Bills prediction, pick against the spread and over/under for Week 8: Baltimore's Maryland Science Center spends Sunday morning launching jack-o'-lanterns off its roof at the Pumpkin Smash, and by 1 p.m. the Ravens will find out whether their defense can do the same to Josh Allen in Orchard Park. Buffalo is off a bye, Lamar Jackson is back, and I'm laying the 3 anyway.

Kickoff is 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS from Highmark Stadium. The consensus has Buffalo −3 with a total of 54.5 as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET, and my card reads Buffalo Bills −3, Under 54.5, with a final of Bills 29, Ravens 24.

The Bills side starts with the calendar. Buffalo last played in Week 6 at Las Vegas and comes in off a bye. Baltimore played Cincinnati at home last Sunday and has a normal week. The Bills are 5-1 with 197 points scored in six games, and they have been better on the road (3-0) than at home (2-1).

The Formula: Net ratings Buffalo Bills 2.2, Baltimore Ravens −2.0 (nflverse play-by-play, Oct 28, 2026).

Its card has Buffalo winning by seven, and the Bills are asked to lay only 3.

The ground game agrees. Buffalo runs for 5.4 yards a carry against a Baltimore defense that allows 3.9, and Baltimore's protection has been the shakiest thing on the field: about one sack every twelve dropbacks. Tyler Huntley started the Cincinnati game for the Ravens, but he's not the quarterback I'm handicapping. Lamar Jackson was a full participant on Wednesday's official injury report and is expected back, and Josh Allen started Buffalo's last game before the bye. The bigger Baltimore worry is on defense: Roquan Smith, Kyle Hamilton and Calais Campbell all sat out Wednesday.

Baltimore can run too, and that is where this could go wrong. The Ravens get 4.8 a carry against a Buffalo defense that also allows 3.9, and they are 3-1 away from home. Buffalo's rush only gets home about once every twenty-five dropbacks, so Lamar Jackson won't be running for his life. If Baltimore controls the clock, this stays a field goal game.

As for the total, the Under, because the posted 54.5 already assumes both offenses hit their best day. My final is 53, a point and a half shy, and two teams that can run the ball shorten the game.

The room splits right down the middle on the side. The Formula has Buffalo by 7 and Letdown Watch has Bills 30, Ravens 21, and both lay the 3. Next Man Up has Bills 27, Ravens 25 and In The Trenches has Bills 28, Ravens 26, and both would take Baltimore with the points. On the total, three of the four sit below 54.5, and only The Formula goes over. Follow The Money has no side pick and likes the Over 54.5.

Baltimore's pumpkins come off the Science Center roof a few hours before kickoff, and the Ravens' pocket looks like the next thing to fall. A rested home team running at 5.4 a carry against protection that gives up sacks is worth a field goal.

Bills 29, Ravens 24. Bills cover the 3. Under 54.5.

Baltimore Ravens vs Buffalo Bills in Week 8 gets the first Sunday of standard time at Highmark Stadium, with Lamar Jackson practicing fully and Josh Allen rested off a bye. While Ellen Marsh spent the off week walking Science Stadium, the Buffalo Museum of Science exhibit built with the Bills, Sabres and Bandits, Owen Pratt was back in Baltimore circling the Maryland Science Center's Pumpkin Smash, where people fling their jack-o'-lanterns off the roof the morning after Halloween, and he arrived in Orchard Park sure his defense would do the same to Buffalo's January dreams.

Owen: I'll miss it for this. Somewhere on the Inner Harbor a pumpkin is falling off a roof without me, Ellen, and I'd like you to know what I gave up.

Ellen: You gave up a pumpkin. We gave up two weeks of football waiting for you. Buffalo is 5-1, 3-0 on the road, and Joe Brady had the whole staff in the building drawing up plays while your guys were icing their knees from Cincinnati.

Tennessee Titans vs Cincinnati Bengals is Cam Ward against Joe Burrow in Week 8, 1 p.m. Eastern at Paycor Stadium on the first Sunday back on standard time. Cincinnati spends the weekend at the zoo's HallZOOween and at TQL Stadium, where FC Cincinnati plays the Philadelphia Union on Saturday, while Pete Varga's East Nashville neighbors in Five Points will still be sweeping up after All Hallows East, and Pete has come to tell Laura Kessel's Bengals that growth beats a better record.

Pete: Laura, I left a street party for this. Costumes, live music, the whole neighborhood out until ten. I'm here because I'm committed to growth.

Laura Kessel, who has believed for years that every football question is really a quarterback question, did not look up from her notes.

Laura: You're here because Burrow is here. Sit down. Tennessee is 1-6, 0-4 at home and 1-2 on the road. Cincinnati is 4-2, 3-1 away and 1-1 in this building, with 163 points scored and only 122 allowed.

Pete: And 108 scored, 156 allowed for us. I know the figures. Our one win came on the road, which is why I'm cheerful in your parking lot.

Burrow started the Bengals' last game, at Baltimore. Ward started the Titans' last game, at home against Cleveland. Pete judges the Titans by growth rather than wins, which is a handy philosophy at 1-6, and Ward is the whole reason he keeps the philosophy.

Pete: You don't judge a rebuild by October.

Laura: I judge everything by October. That's when a quarterback tells you who he is.

The family histories make a better argument than the standings do. Pete gets two AFL championships, the first two ever played, from the Houston Oiler years, plus Earl Campbell, Ken Houston, Mike Munchak and George Blanda. Laura answers with three AFC titles and Anthony Muñoz, Forrest Gregg and Dick LeBeau, then adds Ken Riley and his sixty-five career interceptions, voted into the Hall of Fame decades late.

Pete: Charlie Joiner.

Laura: Ours too. We split him like a custody arrangement.

Pete: Then we get him on Sundays.

Both defenses set up in a 4-3 base. Robert Saleh runs Tennessee, with Gus Bradley calling the defense and Brian Daboll the offense. Zac Taylor runs Cincinnati, with Al Golden on defense and Dan Pitcher on offense. Neither club runs it well: Cincinnati gets 3.8 yards a carry against a Tennessee defense allowing 4.4, and Tennessee gets 4.0 against a Cincinnati defense allowing 4.9.

Laura: When neither team can run, the man throwing it decides the afternoon. That's not a slogan, Pete, that's arithmetic.

Pete: Jeffery Simmons knows where to find your man throwing it.

That's the part that worries Pete. Cincinnati's rush gets a sack about once every ten dropbacks. Tennessee's blockers allow one about once every twenty-three, which is respectable, and Tennessee's rush gets home about once every fourteen against a Cincinnati front that allows one about once every twenty-three.

Pete: Once every ten is a lot of knocks for a young quarterback.

Laura: Getting knocked down and getting up again is the growth part. Your word, not mine.

Pete: You've been saving that since Monday.

Wednesday's practice report kept both quarterbacks clear, and nobody in this game has a game status yet. Ja'Marr Chase did not practice, which made Laura very quiet for about four seconds. Tyjae Spears sat out for Tennessee.

Laura: If Chase can't go, Joe has to carry 3.8 yards a carry on his arm. I'll admit that much.

Pete: Then I'll admit one thing back. I'd trade the whole Five Points party for one Ward touchdown drive at the end of this one.

Laura: Stick to the sheet, Pete. No rumors. House rule.

The zoo's pumpkins will be gone by Monday. Laura expects Tennessee's road optimism to be gone first.

My call: Bengals 27, Titans 18.

Minnesota Vikings vs Detroit Lions is the unbeaten Vikings, 6-0 with Kyler Murray, against Jared Goff's Lions, 4-2 and unbeaten at Ford Field, in Week 8 at 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox. Downtown Detroit spends the same weekend hosting Youmacon at Huntington Place, so Erik Dahl, who left a Minneapolis Halloween weekend headlined by Wobbleween at the Armory, will share downtown with anime fans in full costume and pretend he isn't enjoying it, while Martin Sorensen insists the only costume that matters Sunday is Honolulu blue.

Martin Sorensen met him outside the stadium.

Martin: Erik, you're 6-0. Smile once. The cosplayers are smiling, and they don't even have a team in this.

Erik: Six games is a slightly louder rumor than five. We won the NFL championship in the nineteen sixty-nine season, made three NFC title runs in the seventies and have never won a Super Bowl. I'll smile in January.

Erik refuses to get excited about any Vikings start before January, and he has history on his side. Martin runs on one idea: a team's window doesn't stay open forever, and Detroit's is open right now.

Martin: The window is a clock. You win now. Detroit won four NFL championships, the last in nineteen fifty-seven, and I'm done waiting for the fifth.

Erik: None since the Eisenhower years, and I'm the gloomy one.

Martin: Back-to-back NFC North titles. Dan Campbell turned this place around.

Erik offered Fran Tarkenton, Paul Krause, Warren Moon and, quietly, Brett Favre, who sits on the Vikings' Hall of Fame list too. Martin answered with Lem Barney, Dutch Clark and Jack Christiansen.

Minnesota has scored 125 points and allowed only 74, going 3-0 at home and 3-0 on the road. Detroit has scored 184 and allowed 165, 3-0 at home and 1-2 away. Murray started the Vikings' last game, at home against Indianapolis. Goff started the Lions' last game, at home against Green Bay.

Martin: Nobody wins here this year.

Erik: Nobody beats us anywhere. Also a rumor.

Kevin O'Connell runs Minnesota, with Brian Flores calling a defense that sets up in a 3-4 base. Campbell's Lions play a 4-3 for Kelvin Sheppard, with Drew Petzing calling the offense. The ground game is dead even: Minnesota runs for 4.3 yards a carry, Detroit for 4.4, and both defenses allow 4.2.

So this one gets decided in the pocket, where the numbers turn wild. Minnesota's rush gets a sack about once every nine dropbacks, and Detroit's blockers allow one about once every twenty-one. Minnesota's quarterbacks, though, have been sacked about once every ten dropbacks, and Detroit's rush gets there about once every thirteen.

Erik: Andrew Van Ginkel and Dallas Turner coming off the outside. Goff is going to see purple in his sleep.

Martin: Aidan Hutchinson sees Murray first. And when Goff gets a second, he has Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sam LaPorta and Jahmyr Gibbs.

Erik: Justin Jefferson would like a word.

Martin: He can have a word. We'll keep the scoreboard.

Then Martin read Wednesday's official practice report and lost some of his swagger. Hutchinson, Penei Sewell, St. Brown and Gibbs all sat out for Detroit. Aaron Jones sat out for Minnesota. Nobody has a game status yet, and Erik was asked not to gloat. He is a Vikings fan; he doesn't know how.

Martin: If all four of mine are out there Sunday, this building gets loud enough to rattle the convention center.

Erik: And if they aren't?

Martin: Then I take a long walk by the Detroit River and come back angry.

Erik: If we win, it's seven games. Still a rumor.

Martin: The clock is ticking, Erik.

Erik: It always is. That's why I don't celebrate in November.

Youmacon packs up Sunday evening a few blocks away. One of these two fan bases will be leaving downtown in a much better mood than the other.

My call: Lions 23, Vikings 22.

Las Vegas Raiders vs New York Jets lands on the same Sunday as the fifty-fifth New York City Marathon, so while runners cross the Verrazzano, Geno Smith and the Jets host Kirk Cousins, Maxx Crosby and the Raiders at MetLife Stadium in Week 8, 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox. This year's marathon marks fifty years of the five-borough course and brings the first route change in fifteen years, a new stretch through the Bronx, which Mike Lasker treats as personal vindication and Vic Moreno treats as proof that New York will reroute anything except its losing streaks.

Mike: Fifty years of everybody calling that course untouchable, and now they change it. Never trust a consensus, Vic.

Mike trusts nothing the experts agree on, and he keeps Super Bowl III as his proof: everybody gave the Jets no chance, Joe Namath said they'd win, and they won. Vic Moreno decides what any Raiders game means by checking who is on the other sideline, and he flew across the country without circling this one.

Vic: It's the Jets, Mike. Nobody in Las Vegas planned a weekend around this.

Mike: Half of this region planned a weekend around getting to Jersey with the bridges closed. Respect the commute.

Vic has three Super Bowls in eight seasons, XI, XV and XVIII, and a defense's worth of Hall of Famers: Jim Otto, Art Shell, Gene Upshaw, Ted Hendricks, Willie Brown. Mike counters with Curtis Martin and Don Maynard, and he will mention, every time, that Brett Favre played for the Jets too.

Vic: We've packed the vans a few times. Oakland, Los Angeles, Oakland, Las Vegas. A football team is a football team wherever the stadium is.

Mike: Our stadium is in New Jersey and our name says New York. We're the last people to lecture anybody on geography.

Las Vegas is 3-4, 1-3 at home and 2-1 on the road, with 183 points scored and 197 allowed. The Jets are 2-5, 1-2 at home and 1-3 away, with 137 scored and 150 allowed. Cousins started the Raiders' last game, at home against the Rams. Smith started the Jets' last game, at home against Miami.

Vic: Two and one on the road. My guys like a trip.

Mike: So do the other team's running backs. That defense allows 5.2 a carry.

He's right about that, and it's the softest figure in the matchup. Klint Kubiak runs Las Vegas, with Rob Leonard calling a 3-4 defense. Aaron Glenn runs the Jets, with Brian Duker running a 4-3 and Frank Reich calling the offense. Las Vegas runs for 3.2 yards a carry against a Jets defense allowing 4.3. The Jets run for 3.9, and that 5.2 is waiting for Breece Hall.

The pocket tells two different stories. The Raiders protect well, allowing a sack about once every twenty-eight dropbacks. The Jets do not, allowing one about once every eleven. The Raiders' rush gets home about once every fourteen and a half dropbacks, the Jets' about once every twelve.

Vic: Crosby is going to camp in your backfield like it's a marathon water station.

Mike: Demario Davis and Minkah Fitzpatrick will make Cousins think twice before throwing to Brock Bowers.

Vic: Ashton Jeanty. Think about that one.

Mike: Hall and Garrett Wilson. I think about them constantly.

Wednesday's official report was mostly practice-sheet business: no game statuses, no quarterback on it. Bowers was limited. Davis sat out for the Jets, and Hall was limited. Mike says the experts will overreact. Vic says Mike is the experts.

Mike: Everybody says this game doesn't matter. That's exactly why it will.

Vic: Everybody says that about every Jets game.

Mike: And everybody is usually wrong. Fifty years on one marathon course, and somebody still found a new way through the Bronx. Super Bowl III. Look it up.

The marathon finishers will be in Central Park by the fourth quarter. Mike plans to finish this one smiling, which in his house means everybody else was wrong.

My call: Jets 24, Raiders 21.

Browns vs Steelers prediction, pick against the spread and over/under for Week 8: Acrisure Stadium hosts Pitt and Georgia Tech at 7:30 Saturday night, then flips back for two 5-2 AFC North teams on Sunday afternoon. Both are unbeaten at home, the spread is 3.5 in a rivalry game with a total under 40, and that half point past the field goal is why I'm with Cleveland.

CBS has the 1 p.m. Eastern kickoff. The consensus has Pittsburgh −3.5 with a total of 39.5 as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET. My card: Cleveland Browns +3.5, Over 39.5, final Steelers 22, Browns 19.

Cleveland is the side because of that hook, and because these teams are almost the same team.

The Formula: Net ratings Pittsburgh Steelers −5.6, Cleveland Browns −5.9 (nflverse play-by-play, Oct 28, 2026).

In a game this tight, 3.5 is a gift. Pittsburgh has scored 153 and allowed 138 in seven games, a modest margin for a 5-2 team.

The rushes match up evenly too. Cleveland's rush gets a sack about once every thirteen dropbacks, and Pittsburgh's gets one about once every fourteen. Pittsburgh's quarterbacks go down about once every thirteen dropbacks. Nobody has a clean pocket in this game, and that tends to keep scores close.

Here's what keeps me honest: Cleveland's record is better than its scoreboard. The Browns have scored 133 and allowed 146, which makes 5-2 look a little lucky. Their quarterbacks have been sacked about once every ten dropbacks. And Pittsburgh runs it well, 5.0 yards a carry against a Cleveland defense allowing 4.6, while Cleveland gets 4.2 against a Steelers defense allowing 3.9. Deshaun Watson started Cleveland's last game at Tennessee, and Aaron Rodgers started Pittsburgh's last game at New Orleans. Neither Watson nor Rodgers appears on Wednesday's practice report. Pittsburgh's defense had a quiet practice: T.J. Watt, Cameron Heyward and Jalen Ramsey all sat out. Cleveland is also on its second straight road trip.

The Over is the cheaper call. This is the one total where the whole room agrees with me. The posted 39.5 is a very low number, the Formula's is about 40, and my final adds up to 41. Pittsburgh's run game and two leaky pockets produce just enough short fields to clear it.

Letdown Watch is the outlier at Steelers 23, Browns 18, the only opinion that lays the 3.5. Follow The Money has no pick.

Acrisure will have hosted Pitt under the lights the night before, and on Sunday it gets two mirror-image teams, a Steelers win by a field goal, and a number half a point too big. I'll take it.

Cleveland Browns vs Pittsburgh Steelers is a 5-2 against 5-2 AFC North fight in Week 8, Deshaun Watson and Todd Monken against Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy, 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS. Acrisure Stadium gets no rest for it: at 7:30 Saturday night the same field hosts Pitt against Georgia Tech, so the grounds crew gets one overnight to turn it back into a Steelers field before Frank Haller walks in from the North Shore to tell Ed Kowalski that Cleveland's eight titles still outrank six Lombardis.

Ed Kowalski measures every franchise by how long it keeps its people, and he likes that the building works double shifts.

Ed: Pitt on Saturday, the Steelers on Sunday, same field, same rivers. That's continuity, Frank. Chuck Noll coached here for more than two decades and never held another head coaching job.

Frank: You say that like it's a personality.

Frank will remind anyone in earshot that Cleveland was the gold standard before the Super Bowl existed, and he left a Halloween show by Mushroomhead, Cleveland's own masked metal band, at the Agora to make the drive.

Frank: Before nineteen sixty-five, Ed. Four AAFC championships in a row, then four NFL championships. We ran this league while your team waited on its first title.

Ed: Six Super Bowls. IX, X, XIII, XIV, XL, XLIII.

Frank: I'll give you six. I won't give anybody the Factory of Sadness.

Ed: The Immaculate Reception. Fourth down, twenty-two seconds left, down a point to the Raiders. And the Steel Curtain team in the bicentennial season started one and four, then posted five shutouts in its last nine games.

Frank: Still not eight championships.

Ed: Mel Blount, Terry Bradshaw, Alan Faneca, Dermontti Dawson. I can keep going until kickoff.

These teams are mirror images. Both are 3-0 at home and 2-2 on the road. Cleveland has scored 133 points and allowed 146; Pittsburgh has scored 153 and allowed 138. Watson started the Browns' last game, at Tennessee. Rodgers started the Steelers' last game, at New Orleans. Cleveland makes its second straight road trip.

Ed: You've allowed more than you scored and you're 5-2. That's a lucky penny.

Frank: Wins are wins. Nobody asks how.

Monken has Mike Rutenberg calling a 4-3 defense. McCarthy has Patrick Graham calling a 3-4. Pittsburgh runs for 5.0 yards a carry against a Cleveland defense allowing 4.6. Cleveland runs for 4.2 against a Steelers defense allowing only 3.9, which is why Frank keeps talking about the past.

The pocket is a mosh pit on both sides, the kind Mushroomhead would recognize. Cleveland's quarterbacks have been sacked about once every ten dropbacks, and Pittsburgh's rush gets there about once every fourteen. Pittsburgh's quarterbacks go down about once every thirteen dropbacks, and Cleveland's rush gets home about once every thirteen.

Ed: T.J. Watt and Cameron Heyward. Watson will hear footsteps in his sleep.

Frank: Jared Verse and Mason Graham will be visiting Rodgers. Denzel Ward will be waiting on anything thrown his way.

Ed: Patrick Queen in the middle. He likes this rivalry.

Frank: Everybody in Cleveland likes this rivalry. We just like it more when we win it.

Wednesday's official practice report hit both defenses. Watt, Heyward and Jalen Ramsey all sat out for Pittsburgh, Verse sat out for Cleveland, and nobody in this game has a game status yet. If Watt and Heyward are both cleared, Ed expects that 3.9 to hold. If not, Frank's 4.2 starts to look like a plan.

Frank: Last thing. McCarthy. How long does he get?

Ed: If he stays as long as Noll, I'll be very old and very happy.

The Pitt crowd will have left the place loud. Ed wants it louder by four o'clock, and Frank wants it quiet enough to hear the Browns celebrating.

My call: Steelers 22, Browns 19.

Ivy: We did it in one fewer game.

Lou insists the Colts are one franchise from Baltimore to Indianapolis, and he will argue it at any tailgate in Duval County. The Colts make their second straight road trip here, but his history travels with him: the NFL championship in the fifty-eight season, the one people still call the greatest game ever played, with Raymond Berry catching everything.

Lou: Three NFL championships before the merger. Super Bowl V and Super Bowl XLI. Art Donovan, Marvin Harrison, Dwight Freeney, Eric Dickerson, Marshall Faulk. I don't start counting when the moving trucks crossed into Indiana.

Ivy: Tony Boselli. One Hall of Famer, and he's the one this franchise points to first. We're younger. We're still writing our list.

Lou: In pencil.

Ivy: And you keep yours in an attic.

Lou: That one landed.

Lawrence started the Jaguars' last game, at home against Houston, before the bye. Jones started the Colts' last game, at Minnesota.

Shane Steichen runs Indianapolis, with Lou Anarumo calling a 4-3 defense and Jim Bob Cooter running the offense. Liam Coen runs Jacksonville, with Anthony Campanile calling a 4-3 and Grant Udinski on offense. The toughest group in this game is Jacksonville's run defense, allowing only 3.3 yards a carry, and Indianapolis runs for 4.2. Going the other way, Jacksonville runs for 4.3 against an Indianapolis defense allowing 5.1, which is the split Ivy circled first.

Ivy: Taylor against 3.3. That's the matchup, Lou. Your best player against our best group.

Lou: Jonathan Taylor finds cracks in walls. It's what he does.

Ivy: Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen will find Jones. And Travis Hunter is on my depth chart. Sit with that.

Lou: DeForest Buckner and Laiatu Latu will visit Lawrence. Sauce Gardner will shadow whoever you throw to.

Ivy: Duval will be loud. I don't do Duval magic, though. I do splits.

Lou: Finally, a numbers person who admits it.

Los Angeles Chargers vs Los Angeles Rams in Week 8 puts Justin Herbert and Jim Harbaugh's winless Chargers against Matthew Stafford and Sean McVay's Rams at SoFi Stadium, 4:05 p.m. Eastern on Fox. Across town, Grand Park in downtown Los Angeles closes its Día de los Muertos celebration that same afternoon with Noche de los Muertos, built around this year's theme, "The Power of One," which the Chargers' Marty Szabo has adopted as a plea and the Rams' Diane Kerr hears as a warning about one bad afternoon.

Marty Szabo, who watches Chargers film the way a detective watches security footage, took the theme personally.

Marty: The power of one, Diane. One win. That's all the altar needs this year.

Diane Kerr reads every Rams roster like a family tree, and she has the branches memorized: McVay at the trunk, Chris Shula on defense, Nathan Scheelhaase on offense and Kliff Kingsbury as assistant head coach.

Diane: Follow the tree, Marty. That's how you win Super Bowls XXXIV and LVI.

Marty: We won the AFL championship in the sixty-three season. Lance Alworth, Dan Fouts, Ron Mix. Johnny Unitas is on our Hall of Fame list, and nobody remembers that but me.

Diane: Deacon Jones, Merlin Olsen, Isaac Bruce, Kevin Greene, Eric Dickerson, Marshall Faulk.

Marty: Deacon Jones is ours too. We share him. We share a parking lot. We share a front door.

Diane: And now an Aaron Donald story. He retired, and he came back this year.

Marty: I rolled that tape too. Didn't enjoy it.

Marty also refuses to say the phrase about the same old Chargers. He'll describe every missed block on film, but he won't say that.

The Rams are 3-4, 1-3 at home and 2-1 on the road, with 170 points scored and 159 allowed. The Chargers are 0-6, 0-3 at home and 0-3 away, with 90 scored and 151 allowed. Herbert started the Chargers' last game, at Kansas City in Week 6. Stafford started the Rams' last game, at Las Vegas. The Chargers had two weeks to prepare.

Diane: I'd guess Harbaugh ran a bye week that felt like training camp.

Marty: He runs every week like training camp. And Mike McDaniel had two weeks to draw up something new.

Both defenses set up in a 3-4 base, with Chris O'Leary running the Chargers' and McDaniel calling their offense. The Rams run for 5.0 yards a carry against a Chargers defense allowing 4.3. The Chargers run for 4.2 against a Rams defense allowing exactly the same.

The pocket is the tape Marty keeps rewinding. The Chargers' quarterbacks have been sacked about once every ten dropbacks, while the Rams' rush gets home about once every twenty-three. The Rams' blockers allow a sack about once every twenty-six dropbacks, and the Chargers' rush gets there about once every seventeen.

Marty: Khalil Mack and, if that hamstring lets him, Derwin James Jr. will be in Stafford's kitchen.

Diane: Donald and Kobie Turner will be in Herbert's living room. And Puka Nacua goes wherever your safeties aren't.

Marty: Ladd McConkey and Omarion Hampton. Somebody on our team will score. I'm almost sure.

Diane: Trent McDuffie would like to talk to Ladd about that.

Wednesday's official practice report had names from both teams. The Chargers held out Derwin James Jr., who had a setback with his hamstring, and guard Kayode Awosika, gave Khalil Mack a rest day and had Ladd McConkey practicing fully. The Rams held out center Coleman Shelton and tight end Colby Parkinson and had McDuffie limited. Nobody has a game status yet. Both of them had excuses ready, and now both of them get to use them.

Marty: If we win this one, I'm framing the tape and hanging it next to a marigold.

Diane: If you win this one, I'm following the tree all the way back to see where we went wrong.

Grand Park's Noche de los Muertos runs until seven Pacific. Marty would like one more thing to celebrate by then, and Diane would like to keep the Chargers' candle unlit a little longer.

My call: Rams 26, Chargers 18.

The stadium lots got their warmup on Thursday, when the Mile High Trunk or Treat filled them with decorated cars and kids in costume, and by Sunday those same lots belong to orange jerseys again, with Ruth Calder ready to tell Chet Morrell that the Chiefs' run of Lombardis means nothing at altitude.

Ruth Calder knows those lots well, and she asks one question about every era: where is the quarterback in his arc?

Ruth: John Elway won his two titles late, Super Bowls XXXII and XXXIII. That's the arc done right. Then we added Super Bowl 50.

Chet Morrell audits every Chiefs season against the Hank Stram teams and the Reid and Mahomes run, and he left Kansas City with the Nelson-Atkins Museum's Día de los Muertos celebration on the weekend calendar.

Chet: Four Super Bowls, IV, LIV, LVII and LVIII. Stram won three AFL titles and Super Bowl IV. Reid and Mahomes added three more. And the audit also lists Super Bowl LIX, forty to twenty-two, Philadelphia. I keep it on my desk so nobody thinks repeats are automatic.

Ruth: Healthiest thing a Chiefs person has ever said to me.

They traded Hall of Fame names like neighbors trading recipes: Derrick Thomas, Emmitt Thomas and Lamar Hunt from Chet; Elway, Terrell Davis, Champ Bailey and Floyd Little from Ruth.

Kansas City is 5-1, 3-0 at home and 2-1 on the road, with 143 points scored and only 103 allowed in six games. Denver is 5-2, 3-0 at home and 2-2 away, with 144 scored and 141 allowed. Mahomes started the Chiefs' last game, at Seattle. Nix started the Broncos' last game, at Arizona. This is Kansas City's second straight road trip.

Ruth: Three and oh at Mile High.

Chet: Three and oh at Arrowhead. Somebody's perfect home record ends Sunday, and it isn't ours.

Reid has Steve Spagnuolo calling a 4-3 defense and Eric Bieniemy calling the offense. Payton has Vance Joseph calling a 3-4 and Davis Webb running the offense. Kansas City runs for 5.6 yards a carry against a Denver defense allowing 4.7, the biggest mismatch in the game. Denver runs for 4.0 against a Chiefs defense allowing just 3.6.

Ruth would rather talk about the pocket, because that's where Denver is loudest. The Broncos get a sack about once every thirteen dropbacks, while Kansas City's blockers allow one about once every twenty-eight. Denver's blockers allow a sack about once every twenty-five dropbacks, and the Chiefs' rush gets there exactly once every twenty-seven.

Ruth: Nik Bonitto and Zach Allen will be in Mahomes' face all afternoon, and Pat Surtain II will be waiting downfield.

Chet: Chris Jones and George Karlaftis will visit Nix. Travis Kelce, Rashee Rice and Kenneth Walker III will visit your secondary.

Then Wednesday's official practice report took some air out of her. Mahomes practiced fully. Allen sat out for Denver, and Ruth changed the subject. Nobody has a game status yet.

Chet: If Allen can't go, the audit says we run it at 5.6 until you stop us.

Ruth: And if he can, your audit gets a footnote.

Chet: Does Mahomes get late-career titles like Elway?

Ruth: Ask me when his arc is done. I don't grade the middle of the story. Bo, either.

Chet: That's an audit I respect.

The trunks are long gone from those lots. Ruth wants the Chiefs' visit packed up with them, and Chet came to Denver to make sure they leave in red.

New England Patriots vs Miami Dolphins is Drake Maye and Mike Vrabel against Malik Willis and Jeff Hafley, an AFC East game in Week 8 at Hard Rock Stadium, 4:25 p.m. Eastern on CBS. Glen Tolliver flew south the morning after Salem's Haunted Happenings closed its month with a Halloween night finale and drone show, and he landed in a Miami still buzzing from Wynwood's HalloWYN weekend, where Carla Ruiz was waiting to argue that a rebuild beats a pile of old receipts.

Carla Ruiz picked him up and drove him past the Wynwood murals on purpose.

Carla: Every wall in that neighborhood used to be a warehouse, Glen. Somebody looked at a broken block and saw a plan. That's how I look at this roster.

Carla treats a broken roster the way a contractor treats a house that needs new floors. Glen treats championships as receipts for work already done, useful for nothing except proving it can be done again.

Glen: Six Super Bowls. XXXVI, XXXVIII, XXXIX, XLIX, LI, LIII. Receipts. They don't win next Sunday. And I keep Super Bowl LX, Seattle twenty-nine, us thirteen, in my wallet so I don't get nostalgic.

Carla: Painful wallet. Miami won Super Bowls VII and VIII back to back, and five AFC titles, and I'm proud of every one. But I don't throw good years after bad decisions.

Glen named John Hannah, Mike Haynes, Ty Law, Randy Moss and Curtis Martin. Carla said Miami's history is real and its present is a construction site, and she said it like a woman who has seen the permit.

New England is 4-3, 3-0 at home and 1-3 on the road, with 160 points scored and 143 allowed. Miami is 1-5, 0-2 at home and 1-3 away, with 98 scored and 157 allowed in six games. Maye started the Patriots' last game, at Chicago. Willis started the Dolphins' last game, at the Jets. New England arrives with ten days of rest.

Glen: Three and oh at home, one and three away. Process says fix the road.

Carla: Our one win came on the road, so home cooking hasn't helped us either.

Vrabel has Zak Kuhr calling a 3-4 defense and Josh McDaniels calling the offense. Hafley has Sean Duggan running a 4-3 and Bobby Slowik on offense. The best ground matchup belongs to Miami, 4.7 yards a carry against a Patriots defense allowing 4.1. New England runs for 4.4 against a Dolphins defense allowing 4.2.

Carla: Ollie Gordon II and Malik Washington. That's the first floor of the new house.

The pocket favors the visitors. Miami's quarterbacks have been sacked about once every eleven dropbacks, and New England's rush gets home about once every fourteen. Miami's rush has been the quietest in the game, a sack about once every twenty-nine and a half dropbacks, against New England blockers who allow one about once every seventeen.

Glen: Christian Gonzalez and Milton Williams will make Willis earn every yard.

Carla: Zach Sieler and Jordyn Brooks will visit Maye.

Glen: A.J. Brown and Hunter Henry will visit your secondary.

Carla: We have room for guests. The guest house is being rebuilt too.

Wednesday's official practice report had Maye and Willis both practicing fully, Brown limited, and nobody with a game status yet.

Glen: When does the rebuild end?

Carla: When the books balance and the scoreboard agrees. Not one day sooner.

Glen: Salem spent a whole month on one night. You've spent longer on one roster.

Carla: Salem had centuries of material. Give me a couple more drafts.

Wynwood was warehouses once. Carla says the Dolphins are a mural in progress, and Glen says he'd like to see the paint dry before Christmas.

My call: Patriots 26, Dolphins 20.

Philadelphia Eagles vs Washington Commanders on Sunday Night Football in Week 8 comes one day after the fifty-first Marine Corps Marathon shut down the Key and Memorial bridges, and Claire Benton, who thinks structure beats talent every time, spent Saturday admiring how Washington moves thousands of runners on schedule. Ray Donnelly, who explains every Eagles result by watching the guards, drove down I-95 from Philadelphia muttering that nobody ever won a marathon or a football game without somebody big clearing the road.

Claire: Mile markers, water stations, bridge closures timed to the minute. That's coaching, Ray. Joe Gibbs won three Super Bowls here, XVII, XXII and XXVI, with exactly that kind of plan.

Ray: Super Bowl LIX, forty to twenty-two against Kansas City. The guards won that game, and I'm the only one who wrote it down.

The trophy talk went both ways. Ray has Super Bowls LII and LIX and three NFL championships before the merger; Claire has two pre-merger titles and the Gibbs years. She offered Sammy Baugh, Cliff Battles, George Allen and Bobby Beathard. He offered Chuck Bednarik, Reggie White, Steve Van Buren, Pete Pihos and Bob Brown, and pointed out that every one of them was large.

Claire: Of course you'd go with the big men.

Ray: Of course I would. I won't take a quarterback opinion as a substitute for watching the guards.

Claire: And I won't pretend one quarterback saves a franchise without a structure around him.

Neither of them is enjoying the fall. Philadelphia is 2-5, 1-3 at home and 1-2 on the road, with 127 points scored and 175 allowed. Washington is 1-4-1, 1-1-1 at home and 0-3 away, with 132 scored and 172 allowed in six games. Tanner McKee started the Eagles' last game, at home against Dallas. Jayden Daniels started the Commanders' last game, at San Francisco in Week 6.

Claire: Thirteen days of rest. Dan Quinn had two weeks to rebuild the structure.

Ray: Six days for us. My guards are tired and yours are fresh. Somebody in this city just ran twenty-six miles, and he's probably less sore than my left guard.

Both defenses set up in a 3-4 base. Nick Sirianni runs Philadelphia, with Vic Fangio on defense and Sean Mannion calling the offense. Quinn has Daronte Jones on defense and David Blough on offense. Washington runs for 4.8 yards a carry against an Eagles defense allowing 4.3; Philadelphia runs for 3.9 against a Commanders defense allowing 4.2.

That 3.9 is what bothers Ray, and the pocket doesn't comfort him. The Eagles' rush has been the quietest in the building, a sack about once every thirty-one and a half dropbacks, and Philadelphia's quarterbacks go down about once every fourteen. Washington's blockers allow one about once every fifteen, and its rush gets home about once every twenty-one.

Ray: Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis are due. They've been due for weeks.

Claire: Daron Payne and Frankie Luvu are due too. Jayden Daniels is always due.

Ray: Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith, hamstrings permitting. And Quinyon Mitchell will be glued to Stefon Diggs if he plays.

Claire: Jacory Croskey-Merritt. Say it three times fast and he's already in the end zone.

The official practice sheet from Wednesday was lopsided. Philadelphia, after a walkthrough, listed nineteen players on an estimated report, with Barkley and Smith among those who would not have practiced. Washington had Daniels practicing fully and Stefon Diggs sitting out, with no game statuses yet, and Terry McLaurin is out for the season with a torn patellar tendon. Claire wants Diggs back for the structure; Ray wants the structure tested without him.

Ray: If we win, the game ball goes to a guard.

Claire: If we win, it goes to the play sheet. Laminated, like a marathon course map.

Ray: The runners got the bridges Saturday. Sunday night, whoever wins up front gets the city.

My call: Commanders 23, Eagles 22.

Bears vs Seahawks prediction, pick against the spread and over/under for Monday night: Seattle Center's Día de Muertos festival wraps up Sunday, and twenty-four hours later the defending champions host a 5-2 Chicago team, rested and laying a field goal. It's a real game, but Seattle is the right side, and I'm laying the 3.

ESPN has it Monday, Nov. 2, at 8:15 p.m. Eastern from Lumen Field. The consensus has Seattle −3 with a total of 46.5 as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET. My card: Seattle Seahawks −3, Under 46.5, final Seahawks 25, Bears 20.

The Seattle case is that the record undersells the team. The Seahawks have scored 168 and allowed only 125 in seven games, and they're 3-1 at home.

The Formula: Net ratings Seattle Seahawks 5.1, Chicago Bears −5.3 (nflverse play-by-play, Oct 28, 2026).

Its card has Seahawks 28, Bears 16. I'm not going that far, but a five-point Seattle win is a comfortable place to stand when the number is 3.

The Seattle run defense is the other reason. The Seahawks allow only 3.5 yards a carry, the stingiest number in this game. Seattle runs for 4.0 against a Chicago defense allowing 4.4.

What keeps this from being easy: Chicago is good, and it can run. The Bears are 5-2, they've scored 180 points, and they run for 4.4 yards a carry, a real number against that Seattle front. Chicago's rush gets a sack about once every eleven dropbacks, and Seattle's protection allows one exactly once every fifteen. Seattle's rush gets home about once every thirteen dropbacks, and Chicago's quarterbacks go down about once every fifteen and a half. Caleb Williams started Chicago's last game against New England, and Sam Darnold started Seattle's last game against Kansas City. Neither team has a name on Wednesday's official injury report, so those are the quarterbacks. Chicago also comes in on eleven days of rest, three more than Seattle.

The Under comes from that Seattle defense. My final adds up to 45, and the Formula's number is 44. Seattle has allowed 125 points in seven games, and two rushes this active stall drives. The posted 46.5 is a point and a half too high.

The room agrees on the Under and splits on the side. The Formula has Seahawks 28, Bears 16, and Letdown Watch has Seahawks 25, Bears 20, both laying the 3. Next Man Up has Seahawks 23, Bears 22, and In The Trenches has Seahawks 22, Bears 20, both taking Chicago and the points. Follow The Money has no pick.

Seattle Center's festival wraps up the night before, and Monday belongs to the champs at home, a run defense allowing 3.5 a carry, and a five-point final. I'll lay the field goal.

Seahawks 25, Bears 20. Seahawks cover the 3. Under 46.5.

games.fanatic_story:
Chicago Bears vs Seattle Seahawks on Monday Night Football closes Week 8 at Lumen Field, Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson against Sam Darnold, Mike Macdonald and the defending Super Bowl champions, the night after Seattle Center finishes its two-day Día de Muertos festival. Walt Brenner, who reminds everyone that professional football started with the Bears, walked through the ofrendas on Sunday and announced that Chicago's ancestors could fill every altar in the building, while Kara Holm, who knows that defending a title is harder than winning one, told him altars are for remembering, not for winning in November.

Walt: Eight NFL championships before the merger, Kara. Bronko Nagurski. Red Grange. We were winning titles before most franchises had a mascot.

Kara: And we won the last one. Super Bowl LX, twenty-nine to thirteen against New England. Every team on our schedule has circled us since.

Walt left a Chicago weekend that started with Boo with SUE at the Field Museum, trick-or-treating around SUE the T. rex, and he wanted it known that his franchise has its own fossils.

Walt: Super Bowl XX. And I won't let anybody tell me that team is the whole story. We were here first.

Kara: XLVIII and LX for us. Steve Largent. Mike McCormack.

Walt: Devin Hester. Steve McMichael. Jared Allen.

Kara: You have more Hall of Famers. We have the most recent trophy.

Walt: For now.

Kara: Exactly. Champions get hunted. I'm not assuming we repeat. Nobody should.

Chicago is 5-2, 3-1 at home and 2-1 on the road, with 180 points scored and 143 allowed. Seattle is 4-3, 3-1 at home and 1-2 away, with 168 scored and only 125 allowed. Williams started the Bears' last game, at home against New England. Darnold started the Seahawks' last game, at home against Kansas City.

Walt: Eleven days of rest. Ben Johnson had time to draw up something special.

Kara: Macdonald had eight. He only needs one.

Johnson has Dennis Allen calling a 4-3 defense and Press Taylor running the offense. Macdonald has Aden Durde calling a 3-4 and Brian Fleury on offense. The toughest group here is Seattle's run defense, allowing only 3.5 yards a carry, and Chicago runs for 4.4 into it. Seattle runs for 4.0 against a Bears defense allowing 4.4.

Both rushes have been busy. Chicago's gets a sack about once every eleven dropbacks, and Seattle's blockers allow one exactly once every fifteen. Seattle's rush gets home about once every thirteen dropbacks, and Chicago's quarterbacks go down about once every fifteen and a half.

Walt: Grady Jarrett and T.J. Edwards will find Darnold, and Jaylon Johnson waits downfield.

Kara: DeMarcus Lawrence and Leonard Williams find Caleb first. Devon Witherspoon will be waiting on Rome Odunze.

Walt: Colston Loveland and D'Andre Swift. We have weapons.

Kara: Jaxon Smith-Njigba would like to meet your secondary.

Wednesday's official practice sheet carried no names at all from either club, which left a Monday night with nothing to hide behind.

Walt: What does a champion owe the rest of the league?

Kara: Nothing. The league thinks we owe it a rematch every week. That's what being hunted means.

Walt: Sunday your city honored everybody who came before. Monday it gets reminded who came first.

Kara: Then remember it from the visitors' side. The marigolds come down Monday morning. By kickoff this whole neighborhood is navy and action green.

My call: Seahawks 25, Bears 20.
